stem:
A school library counted the books students checked out during the first four months of the school year. The results were: September, 420 books; October, 510 books; November, 480 books; December, 300 books. The librarian plans to use the numbers to decide when to order new books.

According to the data, in which month were the most books checked out?
choices: November
October
September
December
September and November (tied)
oneLineConcept: Read every value before choosing the largest or smallest.
explanation:
Compare the four numbers: 420, 510, 480, and 300. The largest is 510, in October.

**Wrong choices**
- "November": November had 480, which is less than October's 510.
- "September": September had 420.
- "December": December had the fewest, 300.
- "September and November (tied)": September (420) and November (480) are not equal, and neither is the highest.

stem:
A physical education teacher claims that stretching every day improves flexibility. She wants to share evidence for this claim with the school's parents in the monthly newsletter, so she looks through several reports for the single piece of information that best supports it.

Which finding would best support the teacher's claim?
choices: Many students say they enjoy stretching before class.
Students who stretched daily for six weeks reached farther on a flexibility test than at the start, while students who did not stretch showed no change.
Professional athletes often stretch before games.
Some students who stretched daily also played soccer.
A daily stretching routine takes about ten minutes.
oneLineConcept: Strong evidence measures the exact result named in the claim.
explanation:
Only this finding measures flexibility before and after, and compares students who stretched with students who did not. That directly tests the claim.

**Wrong choices**
- "Many students say they enjoy stretching before class.": Enjoying stretching says nothing about flexibility.
- "Professional athletes often stretch before games.": What athletes do is not evidence that it works.
- "Some students who stretched daily also played soccer.": This does not measure flexibility and mixes in another activity.
- "A daily stretching routine takes about ten minutes.": The time it takes does not show any result.

stem:
Passage 1: School gardens give children a hands-on way to learn science. Students who plant seeds, measure growth, and record data see biology in action.

Passage 2: Although school gardens take time and money to maintain, they offer real benefits. Children who grow vegetables are often more willing to taste them, and many teachers use gardens for science lessons.

Both authors agree that school gardens
choices: cost too much to maintain
make children more willing to eat vegetables
should replace classroom lessons
can be used to teach science
are useful only in the spring
oneLineConcept: For paired passages, find the point both authors make.
explanation:
Passage 1 says gardens teach science through planting and measuring. Passage 2 says teachers use gardens for science lessons. Science is the shared point.

**Wrong choices**
- "cost too much to maintain": Only Passage 2 mentions cost, and it still says gardens offer real benefits.
- "make children more willing to eat vegetables": Only Passage 2 mentions tasting vegetables.
- "should replace classroom lessons": Neither passage says gardens should replace lessons.
- "are useful only in the spring": Neither passage mentions seasons.

stem:
A weather station recorded daily rainfall, in inches, for one week: Monday, 0.2; Tuesday, 0.0; Wednesday, 1.1; Thursday, 0.4; Friday, 0.0; Saturday, 0.7; Sunday, 0.3. The station uses these weekly records to track whether the area is getting enough rain for local farms.

According to the data, on which day did the most rain fall?
choices: Saturday
Thursday
Wednesday
Sunday
Monday
oneLineConcept: Check the units, then compare the values.
explanation:
The largest number in the list is 1.1 inches, recorded on Wednesday. Check the units: all values are in inches, so they can be compared directly.

**Wrong choices**
- "Saturday": Saturday had 0.7 inch, less than Wednesday's 1.1.
- "Thursday": Thursday had 0.4 inch.
- "Sunday": Sunday had 0.3 inch.
- "Monday": Monday had 0.2 inch.

stem:
In a letter to the school newspaper, a student wrote: "Our school needs a recycling program right away. Yesterday I saw three plastic bottles in the trash can outside the gym. Clearly, students here are throwing away huge amounts of recyclable material every day, and a program would fix this problem."

Which choice best describes a weakness in the student's argument?
choices: It draws a large conclusion from a single small observation.
It quotes an expert who is not qualified.
It uses too many statistics to make its point.
It does not say what the student wants.
It gives equal attention to both sides of the issue.
oneLineConcept: A claim needs evidence that matches its size.
explanation:
Three bottles seen once is not enough evidence to show "huge amounts" every day. The conclusion goes far beyond the evidence.

**Wrong choices**
- "It quotes an expert who is not qualified.": No expert is quoted.
- "It uses too many statistics to make its point.": No statistics are given.
- "It does not say what the student wants.": The student clearly asks for a recycling program.
- "It gives equal attention to both sides of the issue.": Only one side is presented.

stem:
In a survey of 200 parents at Pine Hill School, 120 said they preferred receiving school news by text message, 50 preferred email, and 30 preferred printed notes sent home. The school plans to use the results to choose how it will send reminders about events next year.

Based on the survey, which statement is accurate?
choices: Most parents preferred email.
More parents preferred printed notes than email.
Fewer than 100 parents preferred text messages.
Equal numbers of parents preferred email and printed notes.
More than half of the parents surveyed preferred text messages.
oneLineConcept: Compare a part with half of the total.
explanation:
1. Half of 200 is 100.
2. 120 parents chose text messages.
3. 120 is more than 100, so more than half chose text.
Check: 120 + 50 + 30 = 200, matching the total surveyed.

**Wrong choices**
- "Most parents preferred email.": Only 50 of 200 preferred email.
- "More parents preferred printed notes than email.": Printed notes (30) had fewer than email (50).
- "Fewer than 100 parents preferred text messages.": 120 parents preferred text messages, which is more than 100.
- "Equal numbers of parents preferred email and printed notes.": Email had 50 and printed notes had 30, which are not equal.

stem:
Passage 1: Electric cars are better for the environment because they produce no tailpipe exhaust. Cities with more electric cars should have cleaner air.

Passage 2: Electric cars produce no tailpipe exhaust, but their total effect on the environment depends on how the electricity that charges them is produced. In a region that relies heavily on coal power, the benefit is smaller.

How does the view in Passage 2 differ from the view in Passage 1?
choices: Passage 2 says electric cars produce tailpipe exhaust.
Passage 2 says electric cars are worse than gasoline cars everywhere.
Passage 2 says coal power is cleaner than other power sources.
Passage 2 says cities should ban electric cars.
Passage 2 says the benefit depends on how the electricity is produced.
oneLineConcept: Find the point where the second author adds a limit or condition.
explanation:
Both passages agree there is no tailpipe exhaust. Passage 2 adds that the overall benefit depends on the power source, such as coal.

**Wrong choices**
- "Passage 2 says electric cars produce tailpipe exhaust.": Passage 2 agrees that electric cars produce no tailpipe exhaust.
- "Passage 2 says electric cars are worse than gasoline cars everywhere.": Passage 2 says the benefit is smaller in coal regions, not that the cars are worse everywhere.
- "Passage 2 says coal power is cleaner than other power sources.": Passage 2 suggests coal reduces the benefit, which means it is not cleaner.
- "Passage 2 says cities should ban electric cars.": Passage 2 says nothing about banning electric cars.

stem:
A city transit office reported the average number of riders on four bus routes on a typical weekday: Route 1, 2,400 riders; Route 2, 1,150 riders; Route 3, 3,050 riders; Route 4, 1,800 riders. The office will use these numbers to decide where to add buses.

According to the data, how many more riders did Route 3 have than Route 1 on a typical weekday?
oneLineConcept: Pick the right two values from the table before subtracting.
explanation:
1. Route 3 had 3,050 riders.
2. Route 1 had 2,400 riders.
3. 3,050 - 2,400 = 650.
Check: 2,400 + 650 = 3,050.

**Wrong choices**
- "600": 600 is the difference between Route 1 and Route 4 (2,400 - 1,800).
- "1,250": 1,250 is the difference between Route 3 and Route 4.
- "850": 850 does not match any pair of routes; recheck the subtraction.
- "1,900": 1,900 is the difference between Route 3 and Route 2.

stem:
A neighborhood group plans to ask the city to install a pedestrian crossing signal at the corner of Fifth Street and Main Street. The group's claim is that a signal would make the intersection safer for people on foot. Before the next city meeting, members are gathering information to support the request.

Which information would be most relevant to the group's claim?
choices: The number of accidents involving pedestrians at that corner in recent years
The name of the company that would install the signal
The number of restaurants on Main Street
The year Fifth Street was first paved
The color the signal poles would be painted
oneLineConcept: Relevant evidence relates directly to the claim.
explanation:
The claim is about pedestrian safety. Records of pedestrian accidents at that corner directly show whether there is a safety problem.

**Wrong choices**
- "The name of the company that would install the signal": The installer's name does not show whether the corner is unsafe.
- "The number of restaurants on Main Street": Restaurants do not show anything about pedestrian safety.
- "The year Fifth Street was first paved": The street's history does not relate to current safety.
- "The color the signal poles would be painted": Paint color has nothing to do with safety.

stem:
A middle school tracked how many students used its homework help room after school. Before the school began offering free snacks in the room, an average of 18 students came each day. In the month after snacks were added, the average rose to 31. During that same month, the school also kept the room open thirty minutes longer each day.

Which conclusion is best supported by the information?
choices: The snacks were the only reason more students came.
Attendance rose after the changes, but the data cannot show whether the snacks alone caused the increase.
The longer hours had no effect on attendance.
Attendance will keep rising every month.
Students came mainly to eat rather than to study.
oneLineConcept: When two changes happen together, the cause is unclear.
explanation:
Snacks and longer hours started in the same month. Attendance went up, but the data cannot tell which change caused it.

**Wrong choices**
- "The snacks were the only reason more students came.": Two changes happened at the same time, so the snacks cannot be singled out.
- "The longer hours had no effect on attendance.": The data cannot separate the effect of the longer hours.
- "Attendance will keep rising every month.": The data cover only one month after the change.
- "Students came mainly to eat rather than to study.": The data do not show why students came.

stem:
Passage 1: Standardized tests give schools an objective way to compare student achievement. Because every student answers the same questions under the same conditions, the results are fair.

Passage 2: Identical questions do not guarantee identical conditions. A student who skipped breakfast, or who has never seen the kind of vocabulary a test uses, does not face the same challenge as a classmate who has.

The author of Passage 2 would most likely respond to the claim in Passage 1 that the results are fair by arguing that
choices: schools should not compare student achievement at all
tests should use more difficult vocabulary
students should eat breakfast before every class
students' circumstances can differ even when the questions are the same
standardized tests are fairer than tests written by teachers
oneLineConcept: Find the exact claim the second author is answering.
explanation:
Passage 2 answers "same conditions" directly: hunger and background knowledge make the experience different even with identical questions.

**Wrong choices**
- "schools should not compare student achievement at all": Passage 2 questions fairness; it does not reject all comparisons.
- "tests should use more difficult vocabulary": Passage 2 raises vocabulary as a source of unfairness, not a fix.
- "students should eat breakfast before every class": Breakfast is an example, not a rule the author proposes.
- "standardized tests are fairer than tests written by teachers": Passage 2 doubts that standardized tests are fully fair.

stem:
The table shows the average monthly temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, for one city during four months of the year: January, 31; April, 52; July, 78; October, 56. A local newspaper printed the table as part of an article about seasonal energy use.

Which statement is NOT supported by the data?
choices: April was warmer than October.
July was the warmest of the months shown.
January was the coldest of the months shown.
October was warmer than April.
The July average was more than twice the January average.
oneLineConcept: Check each statement against the numbers.
explanation:
April's average was 52 and October's was 56. Since 52 is less than 56, April was not warmer than October.

**Wrong choices**
- "July was the warmest of the months shown.": 78 is the highest value, so this is supported.
- "January was the coldest of the months shown.": 31 is the lowest value, so this is supported.
- "October was warmer than April.": 56 is greater than 52, so this is supported.
- "The July average was more than twice the January average.": Twice 31 is 62, and 78 is more than 62, so this is supported.

stem:
A company that sells water filters makes this claim in its advertisements: "Families who use our filter get sick less often. In a survey of our customers, 85 percent said their family was healthier after buying the filter." The company is now planning to run the same advertisement in several new states.

Which finding, if true, would most weaken the company's claim?
choices: Some customers bought more than one filter.
Families who used the filter got sick just as often as similar families who did not use it.
The company has been in business for twenty years.
Most customers use the filter every day.
The filter is sold in several different colors.
oneLineConcept: To weaken a claim, find evidence that contradicts it.
explanation:
The claim is that the filter means fewer illnesses. Evidence that filter users got sick as often as similar non-users directly contradicts it.

**Wrong choices**
- "Some customers bought more than one filter.": Buying more than one filter says nothing about illness.
- "The company has been in business for twenty years.": The company's age does not show whether the filter works.
- "Most customers use the filter every day.": Daily use, if anything, supports the claim.
- "The filter is sold in several different colors.": Color has nothing to do with health.

stem:
Passage 1: The printing press, developed by Johannes Gutenberg in the mid-1400s, made books far cheaper to produce. As more books became available, more people learned to read.

Passage 2: Literacy did grow in Europe after the printing press appeared, but the change was slow and uneven. For generations, most printed books were in Latin, which few ordinary people could read, and many families could not spare their children from farm work to attend school.

Which choice best describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage 2 rejects the claim that Gutenberg developed the printing press.
Passage 2 argues that printed books cost more than handwritten ones.
Passage 2 agrees fully with Passage 1 and adds no new information.
Passage 2 adds complications to the link between printing and reading described in Passage 1.
Passage 2 explains how the printing press worked.
oneLineConcept: A second passage may agree in part but add limits.
explanation:
Passage 2 agrees literacy grew, but adds that Latin books and farm work slowed the change. It complicates the simple link in Passage 1.

**Wrong choices**
- "Passage 2 rejects the claim that Gutenberg developed the printing press.": Passage 2 does not question who developed the press.
- "Passage 2 argues that printed books cost more than handwritten ones.": Passage 2 says nothing about cost.
- "Passage 2 agrees fully with Passage 1 and adds no new information.": Passage 2 adds reasons why the change was slow.
- "Passage 2 explains how the printing press worked.": Passage 2 does not describe the machine.

stem:
The number of visitors to a state park each year was: 2018, 40,000; 2019, 42,000; 2020, 61,000; 2021, 65,000; 2022, 52,000; 2023, 50,000. Park staff are using these figures to plan trail repairs and decide how many seasonal workers to hire.

Which statement best describes the trend in the data?
choices: Visits rose steadily every year from 2018 to 2023.
Visits in 2023 were lower than in 2018.
Visits rose sharply in 2020, peaked in 2021, and then declined but stayed above the 2019 level.
Visits fell every year after 2018.
Visits were highest in 2023.
oneLineConcept: Describe a trend by its rises, peak, and falls.
explanation:
1. 2019 to 2020: 42,000 to 61,000, a sharp rise.
2. 2021: 65,000, the highest.
3. 2022 and 2023: 52,000 and 50,000, lower but still above 42,000.
Check: every year matches the description.

**Wrong choices**
- "Visits rose steadily every year from 2018 to 2023.": Visits fell in 2022 and 2023.
- "Visits in 2023 were lower than in 2018.": 50,000 in 2023 is more than 40,000 in 2018.
- "Visits fell every year after 2018.": Visits rose in 2019, 2020, and 2021.
- "Visits were highest in 2023.": The highest year was 2021 (65,000).

stem:
A reading specialist argues that audiobooks can help struggling readers build their vocabulary. She explains that listeners hear new words used in context and pronounced correctly, which may help them understand and remember those words. She plans to present this idea to the district's teachers at a training session next month.

Which finding would most strengthen the specialist's argument?
choices: Students who already read well also enjoy audiobooks.
Audiobooks have become more popular among adults in recent years.
Some students prefer printed books to audiobooks.
Many audiobooks are read by professional actors.
Struggling readers who listened to audiobooks for a semester learned more new words than similar students who did not.
oneLineConcept: Strengthening evidence tests the exact group and outcome.
explanation:
The argument is that audiobooks build vocabulary for struggling readers. A comparison showing those students learned more words directly supports it.

**Wrong choices**
- "Students who already read well also enjoy audiobooks.": This is about strong readers and enjoyment, not vocabulary growth.
- "Audiobooks have become more popular among adults in recent years.": Popularity among adults says nothing about struggling readers.
- "Some students prefer printed books to audiobooks.": Preferences do not show whether vocabulary grows.
- "Many audiobooks are read by professional actors.": Who reads the book does not show any learning result.

stem:
A school compared two after-school math tutoring programs. In Program A, 40 students enrolled and 30 of them raised their math grade by the end of the term. In Program B, 25 students enrolled and 20 of them raised their math grade. The principal must decide which program to continue next year.

Which statement is supported by the information?
choices: Program A was more effective because more of its students improved.
Both programs had the same rate of improvement.
Program B had more students enrolled than Program A.
Program B had a higher rate of improvement, even though fewer of its students improved.
Every student in Program B improved.
oneLineConcept: Compare rates, not raw counts, when group sizes differ.
explanation:
1. Program A: 30 / 40 = 0.75 = 75%.
2. Program B: 20 / 25 = 0.80 = 80%.
3. 80% is higher than 75%, although 20 is fewer than 30.
Check: 0.75 x 40 = 30 and 0.8 x 25 = 20.

**Wrong choices**
- "Program A was more effective because more of its students improved.": Program A had more students improve (30), but a lower rate (75%).
- "Both programs had the same rate of improvement.": The rates are 75% and 80%, which are different.
- "Program B had more students enrolled than Program A.": Program B had 25 students, fewer than Program A's 40.
- "Every student in Program B improved.": Only 20 of 25 students in Program B improved.

stem:
Passage 1: Working from home saves employees hours of commuting each week and lets them focus without office interruptions. Companies that allow it often find that productivity holds steady or rises.

Passage 2: Remote work can free employees from long commutes, but it can also leave newer workers isolated. Without casual conversations in the hallway, they may miss the informal advice that helps people grow in their careers.

Both authors would most likely agree with all of the following statements EXCEPT
choices: Remote work can reduce the time employees spend commuting.
Remote work offers at least one benefit to employees.
Commuting can take up a large part of employees' time.
Where people work can affect their daily work experience.
Remote work can hurt the career growth of newer employees.
oneLineConcept: For EXCEPT questions, find the point only one author makes.
explanation:
Only Passage 2 raises the risk to newer workers' careers. Passage 1 mentions only benefits, so its author would not necessarily agree with this point.

**Wrong choices**
- "Remote work can reduce the time employees spend commuting.": Both passages mention freedom from commutes.
- "Remote work offers at least one benefit to employees.": Both name commuting savings as a benefit.
- "Commuting can take up a large part of employees' time.": Both describe commuting as a cost in time.
- "Where people work can affect their daily work experience.": Both discuss how working from home changes the workday.

stem:
A city budget report recommends: "The city should close the Elm Street branch library. A count last year found that it had the fewest visitors of the city's five branches. Closing it would save money that could be spent on the busier branches." The city council will vote on the recommendation next month.

The recommendation depends on which unstated assumption?
choices: The busier branches do not need any more money.
The count of visitors last year was too low.
The number of visitors is the best measure of a branch's value to the community.
Elm Street has the oldest library building in the city.
Visitors to Elm Street will stop using libraries entirely.
oneLineConcept: An assumption is the unstated link between evidence and conclusion.
explanation:
The report moves from "fewest visitors" to "close it." That step only works if visitor counts are the best way to judge a branch's value, which is never stated.

**Wrong choices**
- "The busier branches do not need any more money.": The report plans to spend the savings on busy branches, so it assumes they do need money.
- "The count of visitors last year was too low.": The report trusts the count; it does not question it.
- "Elm Street has the oldest library building in the city.": The building's age is never mentioned or needed.
- "Visitors to Elm Street will stop using libraries entirely.": The report does not depend on what Elm Street visitors will do.

stem:
A survey asked 100 adults in each of three age groups how they mainly get their news. Ages 18 to 34: online 70, TV 15, print 5, radio 10. Ages 35 to 54: online 45, TV 35, print 10, radio 10. Ages 55 and older: online 20, TV 50, print 20, radio 10.

All of the following are supported by the survey EXCEPT
choices: The number using radio was the same in all three groups.
Print was the least common news source in every age group.
TV was the most common source for the oldest group.
Online use was lower in each older group.
More than half of the youngest group mainly got news online.
oneLineConcept: One counterexample makes an "every" statement false.
explanation:
For ages 55 and older, print (20) was higher than radio (10), and for ages 35 to 54 print tied with radio at 10. So print was not the least common source in every group.

**Wrong choices**
- "The number using radio was the same in all three groups.": Radio was 10 in every group, so this is supported.
- "TV was the most common source for the oldest group.": TV (50) was the highest value for ages 55 and older.
- "Online use was lower in each older group.": Online went 70, then 45, then 20, so this is supported.
- "More than half of the youngest group mainly got news online.": 70 out of 100 is more than half.

stem:
A blogger wrote: "In a survey posted on a popular gardening website, 92 percent of the people who answered said that organic vegetables taste better than conventional ones. This shows that most Americans prefer the taste of organic food." Several readers left comments questioning the conclusion.

Which choice best explains why the blogger's conclusion is not well supported?
choices: People who answer a survey on a gardening website may not represent most Americans.
92 percent is too small a share to be meaningful.
The survey asked about vegetables rather than fruit.
Taste cannot be described in a survey.
Organic vegetables usually cost more than conventional ones.
oneLineConcept: A conclusion about a population needs a sample that represents it.
explanation:
Visitors to a gardening website are a special group who may care more about organic food. Their answers cannot stand for most Americans.

**Wrong choices**
- "92 percent is too small a share to be meaningful.": 92 percent is a very large share; the problem is who was asked.
- "The survey asked about vegetables rather than fruit.": Fruit is not needed to judge vegetable taste.
- "Taste cannot be described in a survey.": People can report taste preferences in a survey.
- "Organic vegetables usually cost more than conventional ones.": Price does not affect whether the survey sample is fair.
